title: Acres Green Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Acres Green wells have a 302-foot median depth; finished well costs modeled at $21,100-$33,100.
h1: What Acres Green Well Records Show Buyers
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Acres Green means looking past the presence of a well and checking the local record. Within five miles, Colorado DWR records include 3,144 permitted wells, but only 609 report a pump yield and 99 report a static water level. That makes the available numbers useful for setting expectations, not for guaranteeing what a particular lot will produce.

The local record reaches across Inverness, Lone Tree, Meridian, Centennial, Dove Valley and Grand View Estates. Acres Green sits over Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, and permits identify Denver Basin aquifer wells throughout this area. A nearby well search, a permit review and a site-specific driller's opinion are important before you buy or build.

sections.heading: Acres Green well depths vary widely
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Acres Green is 302 feet. The middle half runs from 42 to 596 feet, so a bid based only on the median can miss the conditions on a particular parcel. One quarter of reported depths are below 42 feet or above 596 feet, and the deepest record reaches 3,220 feet.

The depth mix is also spread out: 34% are under 100 feet, 14% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 27% from 300 to 600 feet, and 25% are deeper than 600 feet. For a buyer, that spread means neighboring wells are useful evidence but not a promise. Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock can change across short distances, and casing, grout and final pump design should be included in a written drilling proposal.

sections.heading: Most reported Acres Green yields are workable, but verify the test
sections.html:
Among the 609 wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute. The middle half falls between 10.5 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 59% producing from 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 41% producing more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute or from 1 to 5 gallons per minute.

That is a stronger yield picture than many mountain or fractured-rock areas, but it does not establish the capacity of an untested well. Ask for the completion report, pump test information and any restrictions on the permit. A yield test measures production at that time; storage, pressure equipment and household demand still affect how comfortably a well serves a home.

sections.heading: Water levels show movement, not a simple one-way decline
sections.html:
The median static water level is 360 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 108 to 585 feet. Only 99 records report a static water level, so this is a limited sample rather than a complete groundwater monitoring network.

The decade figures do not show a clean, continuous decline. The median was 245 feet below surface in the 1970s, reached 396 feet in the 2010s, and was 280 feet in the 2020s. Those measurements suggest that water levels have varied by period and location, with the recent median shallower than the 2010s figure. Have a driller compare nearby completions and ask how the proposed pump setting accounts for the water level and seasonal conditions.

sections.heading: Permit history identifies the experienced local drillers
sections.html:
Permits have been issued in the area from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year recorded as 2025. Activity was highest in the 1990s, with 527 permits, followed by 509 in the 2000s. The record includes 1,351 wells marked as constructed, while 1,597 report a total depth.

The most active driller names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 527 wells; Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.), with 359; and Hier Drilling Co. (Hier, Peter J), with 226. These counts describe permit records, not a guarantee of current availability or workmanship. Confirm licensing, insurance, references and who will perform the work on your parcel before selecting a contractor.

sections.heading: A median-depth Acres Green well models at $21,100 to $33,100 finished
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 302-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $15,100 to $21,100. A finished well including the pump, tank, trenching and electrical models at about $21,100 to $33,100.

Those figures are planning numbers, not a fixed quote. A deeper-than-median hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, water testing, power distance or changes to the pump system can move the final price. Ask for separate line items and clarify whether the estimate includes permitting, mobilization, development, pressure equipment, trenching and electrical work. The wide local depth range makes an allowance for additional footage especially important.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole exposure and the building plan
sections.html:
Depth and yield are only part of the risk. Mapped environmental sites within about 10 miles include 212 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 18 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 7 historic mine features. Those locations do not prove a problem at a specific lot, but they are a reason to review site history and test the well water before closing and after construction.

Low yield, a dry hole, poor construction or an unsuitable pump can create costs beyond drilling. Septic setbacks, drainfield soils, driveway access, electrical service and the house location should be reviewed before the well site is fixed. Colorado DWR permit conditions control use. Domestic and household permits make up 36% of the records, while stock makes up 7% and irrigation 5%; do not assume a permit allows every intended use.

sections.heading: Use the nearby records before buying an Acres Green lot
sections.html:
Start by gathering permits and completion reports for the parcel and nearby wells in Acres Green, Lone Tree, Meridian and Centennial. Compare reported depths, aquifer names, yields, static levels and construction details rather than relying on a single neighbor. The records name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers for 1,611 wells, Lower Dawson for 351 and Denver for 286; all aquifer categories in this dataset are within the Denver Basin.

For a planned home, make the offer and feasibility period long enough for a driller, septic designer and water-quality laboratory to review the site. Confirm the permit's household, stock or irrigation purpose, arrange a pump test when appropriate, and budget for the finished-well range rather than the hole alone. If the property depends on an augmentation plan or other water-right requirement, resolve that with the relevant water attorney or engineer before construction.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Acres Green, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Acres Green is 302 feet. The middle half runs from 42 to 596 feet, while the deepest record reaches 3,220 feet. The spread is substantial: 34% are under 100 feet and 25% exceed 600 feet. Nearby wells help set expectations, but they cannot establish your exact depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Acres Green?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 302-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $15,100 to $21,100. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $21,100 to $33,100. Access, depth and equipment choices can change the quote.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Acres Green?
faq.a: Of the wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.5 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 59% producing from 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 41% above 15 gallons per minute. These figures are not a guarantee for a new well, so request a test and completion report.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Acres Green?
faq.a: The well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles, mapped environmental sites include 212 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 18 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 7 historic mine features. Those maps are screening information, not proof of contamination on a parcel. Test the well through a qualified laboratory before relying on it for household drinking water.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping around Acres Green?
faq.a: The available static-level data does not show a simple one-way decline. The median depth to water was 245 feet below surface in the 1970s, 396 feet in the 2010s and 280 feet in the 2020s. Only 99 wells report a static water level, so the series is limited and may reflect differences in location and measurement conditions. Ask for parcel-specific comparisons.
